yt.title: Voltage Multiplier Explained | Doubler, Tripler, Quadrupler with Diodes & Capacitors | Analog Electronics
yt.description: Voltage multipliers step by step: the half-wave voltage doubler charging C1 on the negative half cycle and stacking it on the source on the positive half, the output building up to twice the peak, stacking stages into a Cockcroft-Walton multiplier up to 4x, every value calculated including diode drops, and the bug zapper that uses it.

scenes.title: VOLTAGE MULTIPLIERS
scenes.subtitle: Diodes and capacitors that double, triple, and quadruple the voltage
scenes.narration: Welcome back. We've used transformers and switching converters to change voltages. But there's a much simpler trick for making high voltage: just diodes and capacitors. A voltage multiplier. With a ten volt peak A C input, we'll get twenty volts, and then forty. Let's build it.

Our source is an A C signal with a ten volt peak. First, a capacitor C one, in series. Then a diode D one from that point down to ground, pointing upward. Then a second diode D two, pointing toward the output. And finally capacitor C two, from the output to ground. That's the whole voltage doubler: two diodes, two capacitors.

On the negative half cycle, the bottom of the source is the higher side. Current flows up through D one and charges C one. When the input reaches its negative peak, C one holds ten volts. And because there's no way to discharge it, it keeps those ten volts.

Now the positive half cycle. The source rises to plus ten volts. But C one is in series with it, still holding its ten volts, the same way round. So they add up, like two batteries in series: ten plus ten, twenty volts. D two conducts, and C two charges to twenty volts. That's the doubling.

Watch it over several cycles. The input swings between plus ten and minus ten. The output across C two doesn't jump to twenty at once. Each cycle tops it up a bit more, until it settles at twenty volts, twice the peak. With no load connected, it stays there.

Want more? Keep stacking. Each extra diode and capacitor adds another ten volts. One stage, ten volts. Two, twenty. Three, thirty. Four, forty. This ladder is called a Cockcroft Walton multiplier, and it was used to split the atom in nineteen thirty two.

The numbers. In the doubler, C one charges to the peak, ten volts. On the positive peak, D two sees the source plus C one, two times V p, twenty volts. With n stages, the output is n times V p, so four stages give forty volts. But real diodes drop about zero point seven volts each. So a real doubler gives two times ten minus zero point seven, about eighteen point six volts. And the more current you draw, the more the output sags, because the capacitors discharge between cycles.

An insect zapper needs about two thousand volts on its grid. Building a transformer for that would be big and costly. Instead, a small A C input goes into a diode capacitor multiplier, a ladder of many stages, which steps it up to thousands of volts. The current is tiny, which is perfect, because multipliers can only supply small currents. The same idea is used in laser printers, photocopiers, and old television tubes.

Three common mistakes. One: expecting the full voltage under load. A multiplier only gives n times V p with little or no current drawn. Load it heavily, and the output drops a lot. Two: using capacitors with too low a voltage rating. C two has to survive twenty volts, not ten. Later stages see even more. Three: forgetting the diode drops. Each stage loses about zero point seven volts, which adds up in long ladders.

scenes.narration: Quick recap. In a voltage doubler, C one charges to the peak on the negative half cycle, then stacks on top of the source on the positive half, charging C two to twice the peak. Stack n stages and you get n times the peak, but only for small currents. Next, the Schottky diode, the fast, low-loss diode inside switching power supplies. See you there.
